messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina was a 43-year-old married pharmacist who had built a life in the same American city where she had raised her children, yet she moved through her days with the wary precision of someone who never fully felt safe. Her childhood in a Middle Eastern home had been marked by physical abuse from a caregiver who enforced obedience with blows, shouted commands, and the sharp smell of alcohol on his breath. Years later, the smell of alcohol in passing at the pharmacy or in the corridor outside a restaurant would hit her with unexpected force. So would the clipped tone of authority, especially when a supervisor or uniformed person gave her an instruction without explanation. At work, when a doctor’s office called with orders, or when a manager spoke briskly across the counter, Mina’s body reacted before her mind could catch up: she felt as if danger were present even when nothing was actually wrong, her attention narrowed, and she became unable to concentrate on filling prescriptions she had done thousands of times.

What made those moments so potent was the way they pulled her back into the original abuse. Mina described her memories of it as more real and vivid than ordinary life, as though the old kitchen, the raised hand, and the smell of liquor were “right there again.” Sometimes the memory came with such overwhelming emotion that she had to stop whatever she was doing and go into the back room until she could breathe. Other times she could recount what happened in a detached, numb way, saying it felt as if it had happened to a stranger. Yet even the numbness did not leave her untouched; after these intrusions, she would look around for the nearest exit, scan faces for anger, and brace herself for the next order. The memory and the sense of current danger fed one another, and both made the workplace one of her most difficult environments. Because the pharmacy was full of requests, instructions, and the possibility of catching alcohol on a customer’s breath, she began avoiding extra shifts and stepped back from tasks that brought her into contact with physicians, police officers, or anyone in authority. She had also started avoiding situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful, because hope felt exposed to her, as though any moment of relief might be followed by a blow.

As the months went on, Mina came to believe that nothing in her life felt meaningful anymore and that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. She saw her silence, her shrinking world, and her inability to protect herself as evidence that she had failed in her most important role in life. Those appraisals deepened the danger she felt: if bad things always happened and she had already failed, then every command, every smell, every sudden memory seemed to confirm that she was still trapped in a life she could not control. They also made the old scenes return with greater force; when she thought about being powerless and having failed, the childhood abuse felt closer and more complete, and her memories became harder to set aside. The same beliefs made ordinary cues around her more threatening too. A boss’s request, the sight of a security guard, or the faint scent of alcohol on a customer could all become signs that she was about to be hurt again, and she would flinch as if she were in immediate danger.

To cope, Mina hurt herself physically to stop thinking about the event, usually in private after work when the pressure of the day and the old fear became unbearable. For a brief time, the pain would pull her away from the images, but afterward she felt even more ashamed and defeated, which only strengthened her sense that she had failed and that nothing meaningful was left to hold on to. The self-harm also left her more on edge the next day, more jumpy to sudden voices and more determined to avoid anyone in authority or uniform. At home, she kept herself from birthday dinners, family outings, and small celebrations her husband tried to plan, because anything hopeful seemed risky and because she worried that happiness would only set her up for more disappointment. The cost was visible in her marriage and in her work: she had become quieter with her husband, more withdrawn with her children, and less willing to take on the responsibilities that once gave her pride. By the time she sought help, it was after a week in which the smell of alcohol from a customer, a supervisor’s abrupt instruction, and a vivid flashback at the pharmacy had left her shaking at the counter and afraid she would hurt herself again. What brought Mina in now was her fear that she was losing herself completely, and her hope, however faint, was that she might finally learn how to live without feeling hunted by the past.
